constitution_acknowledgment.ceo_directive_verbatim: Do not declare #6 a buyer-grade survivor merely because V6 reported 96.97% aggregate reliability. The artifact itself contains a major warning: the worst-case M3 reliability is only 30%, manufacturing variation is 70%, and the self-test detection experiment found only a 60% weighted detection rate, with sensor-electronics failure completely undetected. That is exactly where the pushing-the-envelope doctrine applies.

v6_state_inherited.honest_assessment: V6's 96.97% is the AVERAGE across 8 conditions. The WORST CASE is 30%. A buyer who reads only the headline number will be misled. V7 must determine whether the worst case is a real failure mode or a testing artifact.

attack_1_mechanism_level.question: Does the SMA phase-transition mechanism survive the worst-case thermal environment of the venous sinus (body temperature 37°C, venous blood flow cooling, thermal isolation degradation)?
attack_1_mechanism_level.what_to_test: At 37°C body temperature, the SMA activation temperature must be above 37°C (to prevent premature activation) but low enough to be safely reached by electrothermal heating without tissue damage. If the thermal isolation degrades over 6 months, does the SMA still activate reliably? If the venous blood flow cools the shunt, does the electrothermal heater have enough power to reach activation temperature?
attack_1_mechanism_level.failure_mode: If the SMA activation temperature window is too narrow (between 37°C body temp and 45°C tissue damage threshold), the mechanism is not robust.

attack_2_sensor_electronics_sPOF.question: The self-test electronics are supposed to detect SMA failure and trigger a fallback snare. But if the sensor electronics themselves fail, detection is 0%. This is a single point of failure. Can the sensor electronics be made redundant? Or is the self-test concept fundamentally flawed?
attack_2_sensor_electronics_sPOF.what_to_test: Model the sensor electronics failure rate over 6 months. If 20% of SMA failures are sensor-electronics failures (as V6 found), and those are 0% detectable, then 20% of all failures are invisible. Can dual-redundant sensors reduce this? What about a passive mechanical fallback that doesn't depend on electronics at all?

attack_3_manufacturing_variation.question: The dominant failure mode under manufacturing variation is 'self_test_fallback_snare_failed_adhesion_too_high'. This means the fallback snare fails when adhesion is too high. Is this a manufacturing tolerance problem (fixable with tighter QC) or a fundamental design problem (the snare mechanism cannot overcome tissue adhesion above a threshold)?
attack_3_manufacturing_variation.what_to_test: What is the adhesion force distribution? What is the snare's maximum pull force? If the snare's pull force is exceeded by 28% of adhesion cases, the mechanism has a fundamental design ceiling — no amount of QC can fix it.

attack_4_prior_art_with_api_keys.question: Does the closest prior art (EP2043551B1 Novate Medical, US11690741B2 Covidien, etc. from V2 audit) teach electrothermal SMA phase-transition retrieval in CSF shunts specifically? If the prior art teaches SMA for deployment geometry but not for thermally-triggered retrieval, the novelty distinction holds. If any reference teaches thermal-triggered SMA release for implantable device retrieval, §102 may fail.
attack_4_prior_art_with_api_keys.api_keys_used: Lens (MA5xaz...), Scopus (15db03...), PatentBear (pb_live_gX5LL...) — inline only, never persisted
attack_4_prior_art_with_api_keys.search_completeness: Lens and Scopus tested OK. PatentBear has no public API (web scraping via agent-browser is the documented substitute per V2_PATENTBEAR_PASSAGE_AUDIT.json).

T1_mechanism_robustness.target: SMA activation temperature window ≥8°C (between 37°C body temp and 45°C tissue damage threshold). If window < 8°C, the mechanism is not robust to thermal variation.
T1_mechanism_robustness.failure: Window < 5°C OR thermal isolation degradation causes activation failure >5% at 6 months

T2_sensor_electronics_sPOF_resolution.target: Dual-redundant sensors reduce undetectable failure fraction from 20% to <5%. OR a passive mechanical fallback (no electronics) achieves >90% retrieval without self-test.
T2_sensor_electronics_sPOF_resolution.failure: Undetectable failure fraction remains >10% AND no passive fallback achieves >90%

T3_manufacturing_variation_ceiling.target: Snare pull force exceeds 90th-percentile adhesion force. If the snare's maximum pull force is below the 90th percentile, the mechanism has a design ceiling.
T3_manufacturing_variation_ceiling.failure: Snare pull force < 70th-percentile adhesion force (28%+ failure rate is a design ceiling, not a QC issue)

T4_prior_art_novelty.target: No prior art reference teaches electrothermal SMA phase-transition retrieval in CSF shunts. §102 survives.
T4_prior_art_novelty.failure: A single reference teaches all limitations: (a) CSF shunt, (b) SMA, (c) electrothermal activation, (d) retrieval/release

T5_buyer_grade_reliability.target: ≥95% reliability at WORST CASE (not average). V6's 96.97% average is meaningless if worst case is 30%.

what_would_constitute_gate_gaming: Reporting the 96.97% average as the headline number without disclosing the 30% worst case
Excluding the worst-case condition from the aggregate to inflate the number
Assuming sensor electronics redundancy without modeling the common-mode failure
Using 'similar' prior art instead of exact passage matches

honest_starting_position.v6_headline: M3 WINS 96.97% on pre-registered ≥95% reliability criterion
honest_starting_position.v6_reality: Worst case = 30%. Manufacturing variation = 70%. Sensor electronics SPOF = 20% of failures are 0% detectable. The 96.97% is an AVERAGE that masks catastrophic failure modes.
honest_starting_position.v7_question: Is the 30% worst case a real ceiling (the mechanism cannot be made reliable under worst-case conditions) or a fixable engineering gap (better QC, redundant sensors, wider thermal window)?
honest_starting_position.most_likely_outcome: The sensor electronics SPOF is the most likely killer. If 20% of failures are invisible, the system is not safe for clinical use — a clinician cannot know whether the self-test is working. This is a fundamental architecture problem, not a QC issue.
